overview"} Chapter 5 made estimates, intervals and tests executable in base R. Here we return to Chapter 4's group comparisons and use R to connect a fitted model with the question it answers. We begin with three condition means from Chapter 4's background-sound experiment and compare selected differences inside stated families. We then examine a six-cell pattern from its feedback-by-practice study and test how one comparison changes across a second factor by comparing two named models on the same records. Counts require a different response model, and the size of a difference between two groups' proportions can be stated on several scales, which we set side by side. The same counts provide a small example of likelihood, which makes a fitting criterion explicit. Finally, simulation examines procedures under a stated generating process, and planning relates sample size to either power or interval width. Throughout, a useful result keeps its data, target, uncertainty calculation and conditions together. ::: Studies rarely stop at one mean. Chapter 4's invented background-sound experiment compares mean reading comprehension under three conditions, silence, instrumental music and music with lyrics, and its second invented study asks how the difference between spaced and massed practice changes across three kinds of feedback. Means that differ in a record differ for more than one reason, so the question is what a stated model and its conditions let us say about several means at once, and what a single answer to that question leaves unsettled. Both studies are invented teaching inputs, so each analysis shows what a procedure reports, not what background sound or feedback does. ## Fit and read group means {#ch06-group-models} ### Begin with the question and records Does mean reading comprehension differ across three background-sound conditions? Chapter 4 developed this question with an invented experiment. Each of thirty first-year university students read the same passage for 20 minutes and then answered a 20-item reading-comprehension quiz, scored from 0 to 20. Ten students were randomly assigned to each sound condition: Silence, Instrumental music or Music with lyrics. Each student supplies one quiz score, so @tbl-ch06-sound-data holds thirty scores from thirty different students. | Sound condition | Scores (out of 20) | |:--|:--| | Silence | 8, 9, 9, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 16 | | Instrumental music | 6, 8, 8, 9, 9, 11, 11, 12, 12, 14 | | Music with lyrics | 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 | : The same 30 invented comprehension scores as Chapter 4. {#tbl-ch06-sound-data tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"} These values were constructed to keep the calculations transparent. They are teaching inputs, not empirical findings about music and reading. The student is both the unit of random assignment and the unit of measurement: the ten scores in a condition come from ten different students, not from repeated measurements of one student. Silence is the natural reference condition, so it comes first. The following code creates the complete data. The factor levels fix the display order, make Silence the reference level for later model coefficients and fix the direction of each subtraction. The course data file `background_sound.csv` holds the same thirty rows with a student identifier; reading it with `read.csv()` and applying the same `factor()` levels gives identical results. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sound_data <- data.frame( sound = factor(rep(c("Silence", "Instrumental music", "Music with lyrics"), each = 10), levels = c("Silence", "Instrumental music", "Music with lyrics")), score = c(8, 9, 9, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 16, 6, 8, 8, 9, 9, 11, 11, 12, 12, 14, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12)) table(sound_data$sound) #> #> Silence Instrumental music Music with lyrics #> 10 10 10 with(sound_data, tapply(score, sound, mean)) #> Silence Instrumental music Music with lyrics #> 12 10 8 with(sound_data, tapply(score, sound, sd)) #> Silence Instrumental music Music with lyrics #> 2.708012802 2.403700850 2.581988897 ``` ::: Each condition holds ten students. The condition means are 12, 10 and 8 correct answers, and the grand mean of all thirty scores is 10. The SDs, 2.7080, 2.4037 and 2.5820, are similar without being identical. Before asking whether a difference is large relative to its uncertainty, we can see each difference on the quiz's own scale: Instrumental music lies 2 points and Music with lyrics 4 points below Silence. @fig-ch06-sound-groups shows every student beside the three condition means. Each point is one student's score, moved a small random distance sideways so that equal scores in a condition stay visible, and each diamond marks a condition mean. Two kinds of variation appear together. The diamonds step down by 2 points from Silence to Instrumental music and by another 2 points to Music with lyrics, while the ten scores in each condition spread across 8 points around their own diamond. Whether a 2-point step is large depends on that spread within conditions, and the model below turns this visual comparison into numbers. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Individual comprehension scores and their three condition means.](chapter_06_files/figure-html/fig-ch06-sound-groups-1.png){#fig-ch06-sound-groups fig-alt='Ten scores in each of Silence, Instrumental music and Music with lyrics, spread slightly sideways so that tied scores stay visible, lie around means 12, 10 and 8. Larger diamonds mark the means; the three spreads are similar.' width=614.4} ::: ::: The figure is drawn with the `ggplot2` package, which describes a graph as a data frame, a mapping of variables to position or colour, and layers of marks; Computer Lab 6 builds it one layer at a time and sets this way of working beside base R and the wider tidyverse. ### Fit the group model and read its decomposition For student $i$ in sound condition $j$, the one-way model is $$ Y_{ij}=\mu_j+\varepsilon_{ij}. $$ Here $\mu_j$ is the condition's process mean and $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is its student's deviation from that mean. Fitting by least squares estimates each $\mu_j$ with the corresponding sample mean, so $\widehat Y_{ij}=\bar Y_j$. The residual is $e_{ij}=y_{ij}-\bar y_j$: an observed score minus its fitted condition mean. For Silence the fitted values are all 12 and the residuals are $-4,-3,-3,-1,0,1,1,2,3,4$. The model separates differences between conditions from differences among students within a condition. Chapter 4's decomposition becomes $$ \begin{aligned} SS_T&=\sum_{j}\sum_i(y_{ij}-\bar y)^2=SS_B+SS_W,\\ SS_B&=\sum_j n_j(\bar y_j-\bar y)^2,\\ SS_W&=\sum_j\sum_i(y_{ij}-\bar y_j)^2. \end{aligned} $$ The total measures deviation from the grand mean. The between-group term measures deviation of the three condition means from that grand mean, weighted by their group counts. The within-group term measures deviation of students from their own fitted condition means. In this example, $SS_B=10(12-10)^2+10(10-10)^2+10(8-10)^2=80$. The squared residuals within Silence, Instrumental music and Music with lyrics sum to 66, 52 and 60, giving $SS_W=178$ and $SS_T=80+178=258$. In @fig-ch06-sound-groups these are the steps between the diamonds and the spread of the points around them. The formula `score ~ sound` tells `aov()` to explain score using the sound factor, and `anova()` extracts the decomposition from the fitted object. \Needspace{10\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} one_fit <- aov(score ~ sound, data = sound_data) anova(one_fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | Df| Sum Sq| Mean Sq| F value| Pr(>F)| |:---------|--:|------:|------------:|----------:|-----------:| |sound | 2| 80| 40.000000000| 6.06741573| 0.006665059| |Residuals | 27| 178| 6.592592593| NA| NA|
::: ::: Three fitted condition means use three parameters. Consequently the within-group degrees of freedom are $30-3=27$. The between-group component has $3-1=2$ degrees of freedom, and the total has $30-1=29$. Dividing each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom gives a mean square. The within-group mean square $MS_W=178/27=6.5926$ estimates the common error variance. | Source | SS | df | MS | F | p | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Sound condition | 80 | 2 | 40.0000 | 6.0674 | .0067 | | Within groups | 178 | 27 | 6.5926 | | | | Total | 258 | 29 | | | | : One-way ANOVA on the thirty background-sound scores. {#tbl-ch06-oneway} The null hypothesis is $H_0:\mu_S=\mu_I=\mu_L$ for Silence, Instrumental music and Music with lyrics. Under independent Normal errors with a common variance, the ratio $$ F=\frac{MS_B}{MS_W}=\frac{40}{178/27}=6.0674 $$ has an $F_{2,27}$ reference distribution when that null holds. The p-value .0067 is the probability, under this null model, of an F statistic at least this large. At a .05 threshold it provides evidence against equal process means. It does not say that every pair of conditions differs, that every kind of background sound changes comprehension, or that the invented result establishes a real effect of music on reading. The next section asks the individual comparison questions. The observed share of score variation associated with these condition means is $$ \eta^2=\frac{SS_B}{SS_T}=\frac{80}{258}=.3101. $$ This is an in-sample variation summary, accompanying differences expressed in score points. It is neither the probability that background sound caused a result nor a replacement for a confidence interval. The bias-adjusted omega-squared of Chapter 4, Appendix B.2, is .2525 for these scores, and the Computer Lab rebuilds both summaries from the scores. ### Express the same fit with indicators A factor with three levels can also enter a linear model as two indicator variables. Let $D_I=1$ for Instrumental music and 0 otherwise, and let $D_L=1$ for Music with lyrics and 0 otherwise. Silence has both indicators 0. The fitted equation is $$ \widehat y=12-2D_I-4D_L. $$ Substituting the indicators gives 12 for Silence, $12-2=10$ for Instrumental music and $12-4=8$ for Music with lyrics. The intercept is the reference mean; each other coefficient is a difference from that mean, negative here because both music conditions have lower means than Silence. The factor order in the original setup makes Silence the reference level. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} indicator_fit <- lm(score ~ sound, data = sound_data) coef(indicator_fit) #> (Intercept) soundInstrumental music #> 12 -2 #> soundMusic with lyrics #> -4 ``` ::: `lm()` and `aov()` describe the same set of fitted means, so they give the same residuals and the same ANOVA table. The formula names the outcome and the explanatory variable; the study's design supplies the independence assumption. A different reference level changes which comparisons the coefficients name, but not the fitted means, the residuals or the table: with Instrumental music as the reference, the coefficients become 10, 2 and $-2$. This indicator representation prepares the named models of Section 3.2. Chapter 7 develops a continuous predictor's slope, and Chapter 8 extends the conditional interpretation to several predictors. ## Ask comparisons within stated families {#ch06-contrast-families} ### Specify the comparison and its standard error Suppose the two questions compare each music condition with Silence: Instrumental music versus Silence, and Music with lyrics versus Silence. In the order Silence, Instrumental music, Music with lyrics, their coefficient vectors are $(-1,1,0)$ and $(-1,0,1)$. Each vector sums to zero. A quantity $$ C=\sum_jc_j\mu_j,\qquad \sum_jc_j=0, $$ is a contrast of the process means. Its estimate replaces process means with the observed group means: $\widehat C=\sum_jc_j\bar y_j$. Thus our estimates are $-2$ and $-4$ points: both music conditions lie below Silence. Calling a comparison a contrast specifies this mathematical form; it does not say whether the comparison was planned before seeing the results or selected afterward. That is additional information about the analysis. For independent groups with a common error variance, Chapter 4 extends Chapter 3's pooled SE, $s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_0}$, from two means to a contrast by replacing $s_p^2$ with $MS_W$: $$ SE(\widehat C)=\sqrt{MS_W\sum_j\frac{c_j^2}{n_j}}. $$ Each comparison uses two of the means, so both have estimated SE $\sqrt{(178/27)(1/10+1/10)}=1.1483$ points. The third condition still contributes to the common error estimate and its 27 residual degrees of freedom. This matters when comparing these results with an analysis restricted to only two conditions. ### Calibrate the two-comparison family An individual 95% interval uses a .05 error probability for that one comparison. The declared family here is *each music condition against Silence*. To cover both of its comparisons with at least 95% familywise confidence, Bonferroni allocates .025 to each two-sided comparison. Each tail then receives $.05/(2\times2)=.0125$. The calibration uses the $t$ reference distribution with the model's 27 residual degrees of freedom [@student1908], giving the critical value $$ t_{1-.05/(2\times2),27}=2.3734. $$ The calculations retain the same estimates and SEs but multiply each SE by this larger critical value. The following code extracts the common variance estimate from the fitted object and calculates both results from unrounded inputs. \Needspace{8\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mse <- deviance(one_fit) / df.residual(one_fit) means <- with(sound_data, tapply(score, sound, mean)) estimate <- c(Instrumental = unname(means[2] - means[1]), Lyrics = unname(means[3] - means[1])) se <- sqrt(mse * (1/10 + 1/10)) critical <- qt(1 - .05/(2*2), df.residual(one_fit)) raw_p <- 2 * pt(-abs(estimate/se), df.residual(one_fit)) cbind(estimate, SE = se, lower = estimate-critical*se, upper = estimate+critical*se, adjusted_p = p.adjust(raw_p, method = "bonferroni")) #> estimate SE lower upper #> Instrumental -2 1.148267616 -4.725318112 0.7253181116 #> Lyrics -4 1.148267616 -6.725318112 -1.2746818884 #> adjusted_p #> Instrumental 0.185869921135 #> Lyrics 0.003408398659 ``` ::: | Comparison | Estimate | SE | Simultaneous interval | Adjusted p | |:--|--:|--:|:--|--:| | Instrumental music minus Silence | $-2$ | 1.1483 | [$-4.7253$, 0.7253] | .1859 | | Music with lyrics minus Silence | $-4$ | 1.1483 | [$-6.7253$, $-1.2747$] | .0034 | : Bonferroni results for the declared family of two comparisons. {#tbl-ch06-bonferroni tbl-colwidths="[34,13,11,28,14]"} Multiplying each raw p-value by two and capping at one gives the corresponding Bonferroni-adjusted p-value. Music with lyrics minus Silence is distinguishable from zero with this familywise calibration: its whole interval lies below zero. The Instrumental-music interval includes zero although the omnibus ANOVA rejected equality. It allows a difference from 4.7253 points below Silence to 0.7253 points above it. The two results are compatible, because the omnibus test and each contrast address different statements. The family calibration has a purpose and a price. Chapter 4, Section 3.3, defined the familywise error rate as the probability that a declared family produces at least one false rejection when every null in it holds. Two independent comparisons, each calibrated at .05, would leave that rate at $1-.95^2=.0975$. These two comparisons share the Silence mean, and dividing .05 across the family bounds the rate at .05 under any dependence between them. The guarantee is paid for in width, which Section 2.3 compares, and in power. Suppose a replication of this study used three balanced groups and took this study's error SD, $\sqrt{178/27}=2.5676$, as its planning value. A 2-point difference would first reach .8 power at 27 students per group when the comparison stands alone, and at 33 per group when it belongs to the two-comparison family. Section 6 shows how such targets are calculated, there with the smaller planning SD of the feedback study. Declare the family from the question before seeing the results; enlarging it afterwards spends that power on questions nobody asked. ### Compare with an all-pairs family If the question includes every pair, there are three comparisons. Tukey's procedure uses the joint distribution of pairwise mean differences under the common-variance Normal-error model. `TukeyHSD()` supplies those simultaneous intervals and their adjusted p-values [@tukey1953]. \Needspace{8\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} TukeyHSD(one_fit, "sound", conf.level = .95) #> Tukey multiple comparisons of means #> 95% family-wise confidence level #> #> Fit: aov(formula = score ~ sound, data = sound_data) #> #> $sound #> diff lwr #> Instrumental music-Silence -2 -4.84703504 #> Music with lyrics-Silence -4 -6.84703504 #> Music with lyrics-Instrumental music -2 -4.84703504 #> upr p adj #> Instrumental music-Silence 0.8470350401 0.2084569155 #> Music with lyrics-Silence -1.1529649599 0.0046975772 #> Music with lyrics-Instrumental music 0.8470350401 0.2084569155 ``` ::: The output labels each subtraction direction. Music with lyrics minus Silence is $-4$, with interval [$-6.847$, $-1.153$] and adjusted p .0047. Instrumental music minus Silence and Music with lyrics minus Instrumental music both equal $-2$, with interval [$-4.847$, 0.847] and adjusted p .2085. @tbl-ch06-calibrations sets one comparison, Instrumental music minus Silence, under the three calibrations met so far. \Needspace{8\baselineskip} | Calibration | Family protected | Multiplier | 95% interval | |:--|:--|--:|:--| | Pointwise t | This comparison alone | 2.0518 | [$-4.3561$, 0.3561] | | Bonferroni | The two comparisons with Silence | 2.3734 | [$-4.7253$, 0.7253] | | Tukey | All three pairs | 2.4794 | [$-4.8470$, 0.8470] | : Instrumental music minus Silence, $-2$ points with SE 1.1483, under three calibrations. {#tbl-ch06-calibrations tbl-colwidths="[17,39,16,28]"} The estimate, $-2$, and its SE, 1.1483, are the same in every row; only the multiplier changes. A larger protected family needs a larger multiplier to hold its familywise error rate at .05, so its intervals are wider. An interval should therefore be read together with the comparison and the family it represents. The all-pairs family also covers a comparison chosen after seeing the means. Suppose Music with lyrics minus Silence were reported because it is the largest observed difference. That choice looked at all three pairs, so its calibration would come from the all-pairs family, [$-6.8470$, $-1.1530$], rather than from the declared two-comparison family, [$-6.7253$, $-1.2747$]. An omnibus rejection does not by itself protect any comparison selected after examining the means. Conversely, a separately specified contrast can have its own valid uncertainty procedure without requiring omnibus rejection as an automatic preliminary gate. The relevant information is the question, selection process and calibration, rather than a universal sequence of significance decisions. ### Check what changes when the variance model changes The common-variance model assumes that within-group variability estimates one shared error variance. In a real study, design information and observed patterns help assess that working model. A small normality or variance test cannot certify it, and ten students per condition give limited information about the error distribution. In these invented data the three SDs, 2.7080, 2.4037 and 2.5820, are similar by construction, and every condition's residuals lie between $-4$ and 4. In @fig-ch06-sound-groups each residual is a point's vertical distance from its diamond, and the three conditions spread alike. For independent groups whose error variances may differ, Welch's one-way procedure provides an alternative [@welch1947]. It is the several-group counterpart of Chapter 3's Welch t test, as Chapter 4's conditions section explains. R selects it by default in `oneway.test()` [@rcore2025]: \Needspace{8\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} oneway.test(score ~ sound, data = sound_data) #> #> One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances) #> #> data: score and sound #> F = 5.5144397, num df = 2.000000, denom df = 17.956056, #> p-value = 0.01358053 ``` ::: It gives $F(2, 17.9561)=5.5144$ and p .0136, beside the pooled $F(2,27)=6.0674$ and p .0067. Welch weights each condition mean by $n_j/s_j^2$, the inverse of its own estimated sampling variance, and refers the statistic to fewer denominator degrees of freedom because each condition now estimates its own variance. With similar observed SDs the two procedures reach the same conclusion at .05, while their p-values differ. Each p-value belongs to its own variance model and small-sample calibration, so the two are results to explain through those assumptions rather than votes on which numerical conclusion to prefer. With small groups or clearly unequal spreads, the model choice can matter appreciably. A useful exact identity connects Chapter 3's equal-variance (pooled) two-sample t test, requested with `var.equal = TRUE`, with a two-group ANOVA: $F=t^2$, with the same two-sided p-value. It requires the same records, equal-variance denominator and group comparison. R's default `t.test()` is Welch's test, Chapter 3's last t procedure, and does not meet that specification. Nor is our three-group contrast the same calculation, because it uses residual information from the third condition. The Computer Lab reproduces the matched identity for Silence and Instrumental music. ## Compare a two-way pattern {#ch06-factorial-comparisons} ### Read cells and margins before fitting Chapter 4's second study asks how one comparison changes across a second factor. In this invented study, each of 24 pupils was individually assigned to one combination of feedback (Rereading, Answer feedback or Explanatory feedback) and practice (Massed or Spaced). The outcome is the number correct on a 20-item assessment. A cell is one combination of feedback and practice, and four pupils contribute scores to each cell in @tbl-ch06-feedback-data. The question is how the Spaced-minus-Massed comparison changes across feedback conditions. | Feedback | Massed scores | Spaced scores | |:--|:--|:--| | Rereading | 4, 5, 7, 8 | 4, 5, 7, 8 | | Answer feedback | 6, 7, 9, 10 | 10, 11, 13, 14 | | Explanatory feedback | 8, 9, 11, 12 | 16, 17, 19, 20 | : The same 24 authored scores as Chapter 4. {#tbl-ch06-feedback-data tbl-colwidths="[35,32,33]"} These values were constructed to make the calculations transparent. They are teaching inputs, not empirical evidence that one feedback condition works better. Each score comes from a different pupil; the four scores within a cell are not repeated measurements of one pupil. Repeated patterns in their deviations were deliberately chosen and cannot establish assumptions about a population. The following code creates the complete data. The factor levels specify the display order and the reference levels for later model coefficients. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} feedback_data <- data.frame( student = 1:24, feedback = factor(rep(c("Rereading", "Answer feedback", "Explanatory feedback"), each = 8), levels = c("Rereading", "Answer feedback", "Explanatory feedback")), practice = factor(rep(rep(c("Massed", "Spaced"), each = 4), 3), levels = c("Massed", "Spaced")), score = c(4,5,7,8, 4,5,7,8, 6,7,9,10, 10,11,13,14, 8,9,11,12, 16,17,19,20)) ``` ::: Computing cell counts and means before fitting any model makes the six cells and their denominators visible. \Needspace{15\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} with(feedback_data, table(feedback, practice)) #> practice #> feedback Massed Spaced #> Rereading 4 4 #> Answer feedback 4 4 #> Explanatory feedback 4 4 cell_mean <- with(feedback_data, tapply(score, list(feedback, practice), mean)) cell_mean #> Massed Spaced #> Rereading 6 6 #> Answer feedback 8 12 #> Explanatory feedback 10 18 ``` ::: \Needspace{12\baselineskip} @tbl-ch06-cell-means adds the margins and the three practice changes to these cell means. | Feedback | Massed | Spaced | Equally weighted margin | Spaced minus Massed | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Rereading | 6 | 6 | 6 | 0 | | Answer feedback | 8 | 12 | 10 | 4 | | Explanatory feedback | 10 | 18 | 14 | 8 | | Practice margin | 8 | 12 | 10 | 4 | : Cell means and equally weighted margins of the balanced design. {#tbl-ch06-cell-means tbl-colwidths="[31,12,12,23,22]"} Each cell has four pupils, so averaging the two practice cells equally gives the feedback group's overall mean. Similarly, each practice margin averages equally across the three feedback conditions. In an unbalanced design, a margin must specify its weights: the observed mix of pupils and an equally weighted target can answer different questions. @fig-ch06-feedback-interaction draws the six cell means with one line for each feedback condition. Each line joins two separate cell means; it does not trace individual pupils across repeated measurements. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The practice difference depends on feedback.](chapter_06_files/figure-html/fig-ch06-feedback-interaction-1.png){#fig-ch06-feedback-interaction fig-pos='!ht' fig-alt='Rereading joins 6 to 6, Answer feedback joins 8 to 12, and Explanatory feedback joins 10 to 18 from Massed to Spaced. The lines have different slopes.' width=614.4} ::: ::: The observed changes are 0, 4 and 8 points, so the three lines have different slopes. This describes interaction in the observed means. Inference about a process interaction additionally requires a model and a measure of residual variation. ### Fit the full model, identify its tests and compare nested models Chapter 4 wrote the two-way model as $$ Y_{ijk}=\mu+\alpha_j+\beta_k+(\alpha\beta)_{jk} +\varepsilon_{ijk}, $$ where $j$ indexes feedback, $k$ indexes practice and $i$ indexes pupils within a cell. With the usual sum-to-zero constraints, $\mu$ is the grand mean, $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_k$ describe departures of the margins from it, and $(\alpha\beta)_{jk}$ describes the remaining cell departure. The constraints make this representation identifiable: the effects cannot all shift freely while leaving the same fitted means. There is one grand-mean parameter, $3-1=2$ feedback degrees of freedom, $2-1=1$ practice degree of freedom, and $(3-1)(2-1)=2$ interaction degrees of freedom. Together these describe six fitted cell means. The model therefore has $24-6=18$ residual degrees of freedom. In an R formula, `feedback * practice` includes both main effects and their interaction. We can inspect this rule with the ten Silence scores, 8, 9, 9, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15 and 16. These observations stay fixed. What changes is the proposed center, denoted by $c$. An **objective function** assigns a numerical criterion to each candidate parameter value for fixed data. For a center fitted by least squares, the objective is $$ Q(c)=\sum_{i=1}^{10}(y_i-c)^2 =(8-c)^2+(9-c)^2+\cdots+(16-c)^2. $$ At $c=12$, the deviations are the Silence residuals of Section 1, and their squares sum to 66 squared score points. At either 11 or 13, they sum to 76. Chapter 2, Section 2.2, states that the sample mean minimizes this criterion, and Chapter 3's Appendix A derives the identity behind it. Here the mean is 12 points. A numerical search lets us reproduce the minimizing value without writing it into the fitting instruction. \Needspace{6\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} silence <- subset(sound_data, sound == "Silence")$score loss <- function(center) sum((silence - center)^2) mean_fit <- optimize(loss, interval = range(silence)) c(center = mean_fit$minimum, squared_loss = mean_fit$objective) #> center squared_loss #> 12 66 ``` ::: `subset()` keeps the Section 1 rows whose condition is Silence, and `loss()` returns the sum of squared deviations for any candidate center. `optimize()` searches for a minimum of that function over the interval supplied, here `range(silence)`, or $[8,16]$, which contains the sample mean. The objective is a single smooth bowl over this interval, so the scalar search has one minimum to locate. The two returned quantities have different meanings. `minimum` is the **parameter location**, 12 points; `objective` is the function value there, 66 squared points. The latter is a sum of squared deviations, Silence's contribution to $SS_W$ in Section 1, rather than an SE or an estimate of the mean. The search interval also belongs to the fitting instruction: excluding the best center would restrict which answer the search could return. Numerical stopping tolerance concerns the accuracy of that search; statistical uncertainty concerns what an estimate would do across the repetitions justified by the study. These least-squares identities are arithmetic. An uncertainty statement for the fitted mean adds a model or design and its conditions. Chapter 7 extends this criterion from one center to a line with an intercept and slope. The Computer Lab evaluates the criterion at several centers and narrows the search interval while keeping the observations fixed. ### Change the fitting criterion for a binomial outcome For the completion example, the observations are 32 completions in 50 Online trials. Let $p$ denote a candidate probability of completion. Under the stipulated model of independent trials with a common probability, the number completed follows a binomial distribution. The model assigns probability $$ P_p(X=32)={50\choose32}p^{32}(1-p)^{18}. $$ In a probability calculation, we choose a value of $p$ and consider which counts might occur. For fitting, we have already observed the count: 32 stays fixed, as does the total of 50. We now evaluate the same expression at different candidate values of $p$. Viewed in this direction, it is the **likelihood function**, $$ L(p)={50\choose32}p^{32}(1-p)^{18},\qquad 0\le p\le1. $$ The binomial coefficient counts the ways 32 completions can occur among 50 trials. It is constant as $p$ varies. In this binomial model, likelihood is the probability of the observed data under each candidate model parameter; it is not a probability distribution over that parameter. In particular, a high likelihood at a candidate $p$ does not give the probability that $p$ is true. **Maximum likelihood estimation** chooses the parameter value that makes the observed data most likely under the declared model. The logarithm is increasing, so maximizing the log-likelihood gives the same parameter value. A future study may instead be planned to estimate or detect one particular difference. Consider a future balanced one-factor study of the three feedback conditions, with a declared **two-comparison Bonferroni family**: Answer feedback versus Rereading, and Explanatory feedback versus Rereading. The family has the same form as Section 2's two comparisons with Silence. Keep it, with family significance level .05, even when calculating power for just one of its comparisons. Suppose the comparison of interest has a population difference of $\delta=2$ points. Plan equal group sizes $n$, independent Normal outcomes and common SD $\sigma=\sqrt{10/3}$, the square root of the factorial fit's residual mean square in Section 3. The planning SE for a difference of two group means is $\sigma\sqrt{2/n}$. All three groups contribute to the pooled error variance, so its degrees of freedom are $3(n-1)$, even though the contrast compares only two of the means. Bonferroni assigns two-sided significance level $.05/2=.025$ to each comparison. Dividing that amount between its two tails puts .0125 in each tail. The rejection cutoffs are therefore $-c$ and $c$, where $$ c=t_{1-.05/(2\times2),\,3(n-1)}=t_{.9875,\,3(n-1)}. $$ Under the zero-difference null, the test statistic has the central $t$ distribution already used for the comparison. Under a specified nonzero difference, its distribution moves towards that difference. The **noncentral $t$ distribution** describes this statistic when its numerator has a nonzero mean and its denominator still estimates the common spread. Its noncentrality parameter expresses the population difference in planning SE units: $$ \lambda=\frac{\delta}{\sigma\sqrt{2/n}}. $$ For this alternative, power is the area beyond the same two rejection cutoffs: $P(T<-c)+P(T>c)$ for a noncentral $t$ variable with $3(n-1)$ degrees of freedom and noncentrality $\lambda$. These are probabilities over future studies, rather than a p-value from observed data. Both tails belong to the two-sided procedure, even when the planning difference is positive. \Needspace{10\baselineskip} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} contrast_power <- function(n, delta = 2, sigma = sqrt(10/3)) { df <- 3*(n-1) critical <- qt(1 - .05/(2*2), df) ncp <- delta / (sigma * sqrt(2/n)) pt(-critical, df, ncp = ncp) + pt(critical, df, ncp = ncp, lower.tail = FALSE) } round(c(n16 = contrast_power(16), n17 = contrast_power(17)), 4) #> n16 n17 #> 0.7793 0.8073 ``` ::: The function accepts a proposed group size and returns power. Its first `pt()` call obtains the lower-tail probability; the second obtains the upper-tail probability. At $n=17$, the planning SE is 0.6262, the error degrees of freedom are 48, the critical value is 2.3139, and $\lambda=3.1937$. Summing the two tail areas gives power .8073. Checking successive integer sizes gives 17 pupils per group, 51 in total, as the first size reaching .8 power; 16 gives .7793. This is the power of **one specified comparison within the declared family**. It is neither the probability that both comparisons reject nor the power of the omnibus F test. For example, with 12 pupils per group the specified two-point comparison has power .6328, whereas the omnibus simulation in @tbl-ch06-simulation gives estimated power .9990 against the complete pattern $(6,8,10)$. The hypotheses and rejection rules differ, so these numbers answer different questions. A precision target concerns the interval's width rather than its probability of excluding zero. Suppose the aim is a simultaneous interval whose planned half-width is no more than one point. The family and degrees of freedom stay the same, giving $$ \text{planned half-width} =t_{.9875,\,3(n-1)}\,\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}. $$ This calculation substitutes the planning SD $\sigma$ for the error SD that the future study will estimate. The planned half-width is 1.0078 points at 34 per group and 0.9929 at 35, so 35 per group, or 105 pupils in total, is the first size meeting this target. The realised interval uses the observed $\sqrt{MS_W}$ and therefore has a random width. Choosing 35 does not guarantee that its half-width will be at most one in every study. @fig-ch06-planning shows why a power target and an interval-width target can select quite different sample sizes. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Power and planned interval width impose different sample-size targets.](chapter_06_files/figure-html/fig-ch06-planning-1.png){#fig-ch06-planning fig-alt='For the same two-comparison three-group procedure, power rises above .8 at 17 pupils per group. Planned simultaneous interval half-width falls below one point at 35 pupils per group.' width=614.4} ::: ::: Finally, distinguish the desired number of available outcomes from the number recruited. If outcomes are expected to be available for 90% of recruits, the 17-per-group power target needs $\lceil17/.9\rceil=19$ recruits per group, 57 in total, with an expected 17.1 available outcomes per group under that retention assumption. It is an average allowance, not a guarantee of 17 outcomes in every group or a correction for bias from systematically missing outcomes. The Computer Lab searches the full grid of sample sizes and changes the target difference and the retention rate. A two-group power calculation declares a different study, with different error degrees of freedom, and cannot silently replace this three-group calculation. Choose a planning difference from the substantive question and relevant prior evidence. As Chapter 3's significance-filter example showed, selecting statistically significant results can favour exaggerated estimates; an observed difference from such a selection is not automatically a suitable planning alternative. ## Reading Bridge {#ch06-reading-bridge} The chapter compared group means, separated omnibus questions from calibrated contrasts, and read a comparison that changes across another factor, testing that change by comparing two named models on the same records. Counts required a different response model and their own effect scales; likelihood and an objective function made the fitting criterion explicit. Repetition examined procedures under a declared generating model, while power and precision described different planning aims. When reading a study, identify the question, analysed records, model, estimate and uncertainty procedure before evaluating their adequacy. For a group comparison, locate its subtraction direction and the records it uses. For a test or interval, identify the null, reference distribution and comparison family. For an effect in a table, identify the event and the scale. For a simulation or planning result, locate the generating assumptions and the particular procedure being evaluated. The following concepts were introduced or developed through their R applications here. | Term and common alternatives | Meaning | |:--|:--| | Model formula (R formula) | Notation such as `score ~ group` naming an outcome and the variables that explain it for a fitting function. It does not state whether observations are independent or paired; that comes from the design. | | Categorical effect scales (difference in proportions; risk ratio; odds ratio; Cramér's V) | Four ways to state the size of an association in a table, each answering its own question: the difference in proportions gives an absolute gap, the risk ratio a relative gap, the odds ratio a ratio of odds that stays the same when rows and columns exchange roles, and Cramér's V a unit-free strength, from 0 to 1, for a table of any size. | | Objective function | A numerical criterion evaluated at candidate parameter values for fixed data; fitting seeks a stated minimum or maximum. | | Likelihood and log-likelihood | The probability or density of the observed data under a declared model, viewed as a function of its parameters; the log-likelihood is its logarithm. | | Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) | Choosing parameter values that maximize the likelihood, equivalently the log-likelihood, over the stated parameter space. | : Selected concepts introduced or developed here. {#tbl-ch06-terms tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"} The notation follows the local question. $C=\sum_jc_j\mu_j$ is a contrast, whereas $L(\theta)$ is a likelihood function of a parameter. Similarly, Type II error probability $\beta$ differs from a model coefficient such as $\beta_x$. Observed Pearson $X^2$ differs from the reference distribution $\chi^2$, and $\Delta p=p_1-p_0$ is a difference in proportions. In simulations, $n$ counts observations per stated study or group and $B$ counts repeated studies. An SE describes an estimator's sampling variation; an MCSE describes finite-simulation uncertainty in a computed summary. ### Further reading {.unnumbered} For the linear-model basis of ANOVA, contrasts and nested-model comparisons, see @kutner2005. @tukey1953 develops simultaneous comparison ideas, and @wilson1927 provides the score-interval construction for a proportion. @agresti2018 develops the effect scales for two-way tables. @cohen1988 discusses power and the dependence of a planning result on its chosen effect and procedure, and @cetinkaya2024 develops the simulation-based treatment of operating characteristics used in Section 6.
